There is a particular kind of silence that arrives just after rain, when the air has been washed clean and the world seems to be holding its breath. I like to stand in it, at the edge of a porch or under a tree, and listen to the small sounds that the silence makes room for: a leaf letting go of a droplet, a bird shaking its feathers, the distant murmur of a road that suddenly seems much farther away than it is. In those moments, I remember that the world is not a machine grinding forward but a vast, breathing thing, and that I am a very small part of it.

It is easy to forget that. We live in houses with walls, eyes fixed on screens, calendars and alarms and deadlines stitching our days into neat little parcels. We measure time in minutes and meetings, in how much we have done and how much remains. But the rain does not care about any of that. It falls because it falls. It soaks into the soil, runs along the gutters, fills the low places. And when it is done, it leaves behind this gift: a pause, a hush, a chance to remember that we are not only beings who do, but beings who are.

I think that is why I love walking without a destination. There is something honest about setting out with no plan, no purpose other than the walking itself. The streets unfold differently when you are not trying to get anywhere. A crack in the sidewalk becomes a map. A garden gate left ajar becomes a doorway into someone's small, private world of roses and rosemary. The same block you have passed a hundred times reveals a hundred details you somehow missed: the shape of a chimney, the way light falls through a certain tree at a certain hour, the porch swing that moves slightly even when no one is sitting there.

Sometimes, when I walk, I imagine the lives inside all those houses. I picture a person standing at a kitchen window, watching the same rain I watched, feeling the same quiet. I picture a child pressing her nose to the glass, tracing the path of a drop. I picture an old man in an armchair, a book open on his lap, his eyes closed, listening to the drip-drip-drip from the eaves. We are all separate, and yet we are all in the same weather, the same silence afterward, the same vast and mysterious business of being alive.

There is a line I love from the poet Mary Oliver: “Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?” I think about that often. Not in the urgent, career-oriented way, as if I need to achieve something grand, but in the quieter sense: how do I want to spend this brief time I have? What do I want to pay attention to? Because attention is a kind of love. When we truly look at something, we give it a piece of ourselves. And when we are truly looked at, truly seen, we feel less alone.

The rain says something about that too. It falls on everything without judgment: on the fields and the parking lots, on the rooftops of cathedrals and the roofs of gas stations, on the shoulders of the man who has nowhere to go and the woman hurrying home with groceries. It does not discriminate. It gives itself completely, then disappears. Maybe that is the quietest teaching: to be generous without expectation, to nourish what you touch, and to leave without needing to be remembered.

I am not always good at that. I hold onto grudges like a child holding onto a stone. I worry about things that will not matter in a week, or even a day. I scroll through news that makes my heart heavy, and I forget to look out the window. But then the rain comes. Or the evening light turns golden. Or a friend laughs at something I said, and I remember: this is the texture of existence. This mundane magic. This impossible gift.

So I write, not because I have anything profound to say, but because writing is my way of paying attention. It is my way of standing still in the silence after rain, of letting things settle, of noticing the weight of a single word and the shape of a single thought. It is a practice of being fully where I am—even when where I am is just a chair, a lamp, a blank page, and a mind that wanders like a river looking for the sea.

And maybe that is enough. Maybe the point is not to arrive at some final answer, but to keep walking, keep listening, keep asking the questions. The rain answers nothing. The silence explains nothing. But they both remind me that I am here, now, alive, and that whatever tomorrow brings, I have already been given more than I can ever repay.

So I will keep standing in the rain. I will keep watching the light through the trees. I will keep loving the small things: the smell of bread, the sound of a friend's voice, the way a cat chooses to sit in the sun as if the sun were made for it. And I will try, with the time I have, to be as generous as the rain—to give without counting, to nourish what I can, and to leave quietly, having loved this world in all its broken, beautiful, ordinary grace.
